Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates
Bhat, B. H., & Beretvas, S. N. (2026). Meta-analytic pooling of intraclass correlation coefficient estimates. Research Synthesis Methods, 1–34. doi:10.1017/rsm.2026.10077










Today I’ll talk about my recently published work on meta-analytic pooling of intraclass correlation coefficient estimates, or ICCs.

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates
text:
Overview

Motivation
Review of Concepts
Research Questions
Study Design
Results
Conclusions


I’ll start with the motivation and background for this work and briefly review key concepts related to ICCs and meta-analysis.
Then I’ll describe the research questions and study design, followed by results and conclusions.

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates
text:
Background

ICCs required for secondary analyses:

Prospective power analyses for clustered designs
Correcting effect sizes in meta-analysis for clustering (Hedges and Hedberg 2007) or psychometric artifacts (Wiernik and Dahlke 2020)

ICCs have been used as an outcome in meta-analysis to summarize reliability or clustering effects across studies


There are two contexts that my study is relevant.
First, ICC estimates are needed for secondary analyses, such as power calculations for clustered designs.
For these secondary analyses, researchers often need to assume some value for the ICC usually imputing an estimate from a prior study with a similar design and population.
The second context, ICCs have been used as the focal outcome of meta-analysis themselves, for example, I came across a study where they meta-analyzed ICC estimates to obtain an effect of group therapy.

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates
text:
ICC estimate
One-way random effects model:
\[ \begin{split}
    Level \ 1: Y_{ij} = \beta_{0j} + e_{ij} \\
    Level \ 2: \beta_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + u_{0j}
    \end{split}
    \] where \(e_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma_e^2)\) and \(u_{0j} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_u)\)
ICC (McGraw and Wong 1996; Fisher 1925):
\[  \rho=\frac{\sigma^2_u}{\sigma^2_u+\sigma^2_e}\]

For this study, we focused on an ICC from a one-way two-level mixed effects model normally distributed outcomes.
The ICC is the proportion of total variance that is due to between-cluster variability.
Higher ICC values imply that there is a stronger clustering effect, and an ICC value of zero implies that there is no clustering dependence.

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates
section: Sensitivity of Power Analysis to ICC Choice
text:
Sensitivity of Power Analysis to ICC Choice
Example: \(\hat{\rho} \in \{0.05, 0.12, 0.18, 0.25\}\)























Note. Assumptions: \(n = 20\); \(1 - \beta = 0.80\); \(\alpha = 0.05\); \(d = 0.3\); power calculation based on design effect approximation (i.e., DEFF=\(1 +(n-1) \times \rho\), where \(n\) is the average cluster size)


To motivate why we need a principled way to combine ICC estimates, consider a simple hypothetic example.
Suppose I want to conduct a cluster-randomized trial evaluating the effectiveness of the Marte Meo method on children’s communications skills in German daycares. I plan to use a cluster randomized trial and assume approximately 20 children per daycare and a cohen’s d of \(0.3\).
To determine the required number of day cares I need to recruit for my study, I need an assumption about the ICC. So, I identify four prior studies that have similar study characteristics and outcome that report these plausible ICC values: \(\hat{\rho}_1 = 0.05\), \(\hat{\rho}_2 = 0.12\), \(\hat{\rho}_3 = 0.18\), and \(\hat{\rho}_4 = 0.25\).
Although some of these values are relatively close in magnitude, they result in very different required number of clusters and sample sizes.
If I choose a value that is too large, I risk overestimating the ICC and wasting resources by planning an unnecessarily large study. And if I choose a value that is too small, I risk underpowering the study.
One option would be to take a simple average of these ICCs. However, this ignores the fact that these estimates come from studies with different sample sizes and therefore different levels of precision.
This motivates treating these ICCs as estimates of a common underlying parameter and combining them using a meta-analytic pooling, where estimates are weighted by their precision.
This provides a principled way to obtain a single representative ICC value for use in design planning.

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates
text:
Why Meta-Analysis?
Meta-analysis:

Combines ICC estimates using weighted pooling
Gives more weight to more precise studies

Random-Effects Pooling:
\[\hat{\mu} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k w_i T_i}{\sum_{i=1}^k w_i},\] where \(k\) denotes the number of studies, \(w_i = \frac{1}{\hat{v}_i+\hat{\tau}^2}\), \(T_i\) is the study-specific effect size estimate.

Note. Corresponds to random-effects meta-analytic model with variability from: between-study heterogeneity and within-study sampling error


Meta-analysis provides a principled framework for combining estimates across studies by using inverse-variance weighting so that more precise studies contribute more information.
Similar to many effect sizes commonly used in meta-analysis, such as correlations or standardized mean differences, ICCs are standardized. This makes them suitable for pooling across studies in the same way.
However, there is an important difference.
Unlike these more established effect sizes, the sampling distribution of the ICC is not known. And despite many approximations to the sampling variance for the ICC being proposed, it is unclear which specification performs best when used as inverse-variance weights in a meta-analysis.

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates
text:
Sampling Variances of ICC Estimates


Sampling Variance Formulas







Formula
Equation
Notes




Fisher (1925)
\(v_{\hat{\rho}}=\frac{2(1-\rho)^2[1+(n-1)\rho]^2}{n(n-1)(j-1)}\)
Requires average cluster size and number of clusters


Swiger et al. (1964)
\(v_{\hat{\rho}}=\frac{2(N-1)(1-\rho^2)[1+(n_0-1)\rho]^2}{n_0^2(N-j)(j-1)}\)
Scaled by total \(N\)


Hedges et al. (2012)
\(v_{\hat{\rho}}=\frac{(1-\rho)^2v_2}{(\sigma_e^2+\sigma^2_u)^2}\)
Requires reported variance components and the variance of the level-2 variance


Donner and Koval (1980)
\(v_{\hat{\rho}}=\frac{2N(1-\rho)^2}{N\sum_{i=1}^{j}n_i(n_i-1)\hat{V_i}\hat{W_i}^{-2}-\rho^2\Big[\sum_{i=1}^{j}n_i(n_i-1)\hat{W_i}^{-1}\Big]^2}\)
Requires how many level-1 units there are in each cluster, but reduces to Fisher when balanced


Smith (1957)
\(v_{\hat{\rho}}=\frac{2(1-\rho)^2}{n_0^2}\Big(\frac{[1+\rho(n_0-1)]^2}{N-j}+\frac{(j-1)(1-\rho)[1+\rho(2n_0-1)]+\rho^2[\sum n_i^2-2N^{-1}\sum n_i^3+N^{-2}(\sum n_i^2)^2]}{(j-1)^2}\Big)\)
Requires how many level-1 units there are in each cluster


Fisher TF
\(v_{\hat{\rho}}=0.5\{(j-1)^{-1}+(N-j)^{-1}\}\)
Normalizing transformation; fewest inputs




Note. \(n_0 = \frac{1}{j-1}\left[N-\sum_{i=1}^j\frac{n_i^2}{N}\right]\) is the weighted mean cluster size; \(\hat{W_i} = 1 + (n_i-1)\rho\); \(\hat{V_i} = 1 + (n_i-1)\rho^2\); \(v_2\) is the variance of the level-2 variance \(\sigma^2_u\); ICC estimates are normally transformed using: \(Z_F = \frac{1}{2}\text{ln}\frac{1+(n_0-1)\hat{\rho}}{1- \hat{\rho}}\).



These estimators differ in terms of their assumptions and the information they require from primary studies.
Some require only the the total sample size and number of clusters, while others require more detailed information, such as full cluster size distributions or variance components.
In this study, we evaluate six commonly used variance estimators to understand how they affect meta-analytic pooling of ICCs.

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates
text:
Meta-Analytic Estimation Methods
Assuming a random effects working model with independent ICC estimates, we evaluated:

Robust Variance Estimation (RVE) (Hedges et al. 2010) (Sandwich / Huber–White-type estimator)

Uses a method-of-moments estimate for \(\tau^2\)
Robust to weight specification
Agnostic to distributional assumptions

Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) (Viechtbauer et al. 2015)

Standard likelihood-based \(\tau^2\) estimator
Widely used in meta-analysis



Note. Differences are expected primarily in estimated standard error, not in the pooled ICC.


In addition to the choice of sampling variance, we also consider how the meta-analysis itself is estimated.
We assume a random-effects model, where ICCs may vary across studies.
We compare two approaches.
The first is robust variance estimation, or RVE. You can think of this as a sandwich or Huber–White-type estimator, which provides standard errors that are robust to certain types of misspecification, including incorrect variance weights.
The second is restricted maximum likelihood, or REML, which is the standard likelihood-based approach commonly used in meta-analysis.
Importantly, both methods tend to produce very similar pooled ICC estimates.
The main differences arise in how they estimate uncertainty—specifically, the standard errors of the pooled ICC.

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates
text:
Research Question
How well does pooling of ICC estimates recover the population ICC value:


under a random-effects meta-analytic model,
using RVE versus REML, and
across different sampling variance estimators in the inverse variance weights?

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates

Study Design

Primary study data were generated and an ICC was estimated for each study (\(k\)); meta-analytic datasets contained \(k = 20, 50,\) or \(100\) studies.

ICC estimation at primary study level
Unconditional two-level model with REML







Bias (PB, RPB)
RMSE
SE bias (RSEB)



In the simulation design, we consider two stages: a primary-study data generation and estimation stage, followed by a meta-analytic synthesis stage.
In the simulation design, we consider a two-stage framework consisting of a primary-study data generation and estimation stage, followed by a meta-analytic synthesis stage.
In the primary-study stage, we generate clustered data under a range of conditions that vary the number of clusters, the average cluster size, the degree of cluster-size imbalance, and the true ICC value. Cluster sizes are generated with controlled heterogeneity around the mean cluster size, where the degree of imbalance parameter governs the width of the uniform distribution from which cluster sizes are drawn. This produces bounded variation in cluster sizes across clusters within each study.
For each primary study, we first define a true ICC based on specified level-1 and level-2 variance components. We then introduce study-level variation in the ICC using a symmetric uniform distribution controlled by a heterogeneity parameter, τ. This yields a study-specific ICC value, which is then mapped back into valid variance components while holding the level-1 variance fixed. This ensures that each dataset remains a valid two-level random-intercept model.
This produces study-level ICC estimates, which are then used as observed effect sizes in the meta-analysis.
For the ICC values in particular, we selected a range that reflects different applied contexts.
Lower values, such as 0.05 to 0.25, are commonly observed in clustered data settings like education or health studies.
Higher values, such as 0.50 or 0.90, are more typical in reliability contexts, where measurements within a unit are expected to be highly similar.
This range allows us to evaluate performance across both clustering and reliability applications.
In the meta-analytic stage, we synthesize ICC estimates across studies, varying the number of studies in each meta-analytic dataset. We compare inverse-variance weighting approaches using different sampling variance formulas, as well as two estimation methods: REML and robust variance estimation.
Performance is evaluated using bias, relative bias, RMSE, and relative standard error bias for the pooled ICC, as well as bias for the variance components at the primary study level.

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates
text:
Results - PB for pooled ICC










Here we’re looking at raw bias in the pooled ICC estimates.
Overall, bias is very small across all methods and conditions. The main thing to notice is that the Fisher transformation formula shows slightly more negative bias when the true ICC is moderate, around 0.5.
But importantly, even in those cases, the magnitude of the bias is very small ( at most negative 0.02) so in practice, these differences are negligible.

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates
text:
Results - RPB for Pooled ICC










When we look at relative bias, a slightly different pattern emerges.
Here, the Fisher transformation actually performs the best overall, especially when the true ICC is small.
Across most conditions, we see essentially no substantial relative bias for any method, but Fisher TF is the most consistently well-behaved across the full range of ICC values.

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates
text:
Results - Relative standard error bias (\(\tau_{\rho}\))










This slide focuses on bias in the estimated standard errors of the pooled ICC.
The main takeaway is that the Fisher transformation again performs the most consistently across conditions.
We do see some instability for RVE, particularly when the ICC is very small or very large and when between-study heterogeneity is higher.
But overall, Fisher TF gives the most stable standard error estimates.

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates
text:
Conclusions
Meta-analysis provides a reliable way to obtain a single representative ICC estimate.

REML and RVE performed equivalently for pooling ICCs
Number of studies (\(k\)) had little impact on pooled ICC accuracy
Fisher’s transformation variance formula is recommended:

Lowest bias for small ICCs
Comparable performance for moderate and large ICCs
Most stable standard error estimates
Requires minimal information from primary studies (unlike other sampling variance formulas)



To conclude, we find that REML and RVE perform very similarly when pooling ICC estimates.
The number of studies included in the meta-analysis had little impact on the accuracy of the pooled ICC.
Across the variance estimators we evaluated, the Fisher transformation approach performed best overall.
It showed the lowest bias for smaller ICC values and performed comparably for moderate and larger ICCs.
It also provided the most stable standard error estimates across conditions.
Importantly, it requires relatively minimal information from primary studies, which makes it especially practical in applied settings where reporting is often incomplete.
More broadly, our results suggest that meta-analysis is a reliable and principled way to obtain a single representative ICC estimate when multiple estimates are available.
So in practice, when multiple ICC estimates are available, meta-analysis provides a principled and reliable way to choose a single value.

For moderate ICCs (\(\rho = .50\)), slightly underestimated ICCs when cluster sizes were small, but bias was very small (\(\leq -0.018\)).

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Estimates
text:
Future Directions

Extend to non-normal outcomes (binary, count data)
Evaluate reliability ICCs with fewer level-1 units
Extend to three-level and more complex hierarchical structures
Consider settings with multiple dependent ICCs per study


Because this study focused on continuous, normally distributed outcomes in a two-level random-intercept setting, future work should extend these results to more complex and applied data structures.
In particular, many ICCs in practice arise from binary or count outcomes, where the distributional assumptions underlying both ICC estimation and variance approximations may behave differently.
Additionally, we only considered single ICC estimates per study, whereas in practice studies often report multiple ICCs derived from related outcomes or models, introducing dependence that is not captured here.
Another important direction is reliability-focused ICCs based on smaller numbers of level-1 units, which may behave differently in terms of estimation error and variance stability.
Finally, extending to three-level or more complex hierarchical structures would help generalize these findings to broader applied settings.

Motivation
Common measures for two-group comparisons on quantitative outcomes:

Mean differences
Standardized mean differences (\(d\))
Log ratio of means (lnRR)
Measures of stochastic superiority (\(\theta\))

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of CLES Estimates: A Comparison of Transformation Approaches
text:
Stochastic Superiority (\(\theta\))
The probability that a randomly selected person from one group has a higher outcome than a randomly selected person from another group
\[\theta = P(Y>X)+\frac{1}{2}P(Y=X)\]

\(\frac{1}{2}P(Y=X)\) term handles ties
Several parametric and non-parametric estimators:

CLES, AUC, Wilcoxon U, Concordance probability, Cliff’s \(\delta\)


McGraw and Wong (1992);Hanley and McNeil (1982); DeLong et al. (1988);Newson (2002);Cliff (1993)

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of CLES Estimates: A Comparison of Transformation Approaches
text:
Estimating \(\theta\): CLES

Proposed by McGraw and Wong (1992) under normality and homoscedasticity
Under these assumptions, \(d\) completely determines any measure of overlap between two distributions

\[\hat{\theta} = \Phi\left(\frac{d}{\sqrt{2}}\right), \quad \mathrm{var}(\hat{\theta}) = \frac{e^{-d^2 / 2}}{4\pi} \left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2} + \frac{d^2}{2(n_1+n_2)} \right)\]

There is no comprehensive evaluation on how to best pool CLES estimates

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of CLES Estimates: A Comparison of Transformation Approaches
text:
Meta-analyzing CLES Estimates

CLES:

\(\hat{\theta} \in [0, 1]\)
Sampling distribution is skewed near 0 and 1

Three transformations of \(\hat{\theta}_i\):

logit, arcsine, and probit/SMD

Two back-transformations to obtain \(\hat{\mu}_{\theta}\):

Standard
Integral

title: Meta-Analytic Pooling of CLES Estimates: A Comparison of Transformation Approaches
text:
Back-transformation Methods for \(\hat{\mu}_{\theta}\)
Two approaches to estimate \(\mu_{\theta}\) after pooling on the transformed scale:

Standard:

Returns the median of the distribution of true effects, not the mean (Jensen’s inequality)

Integral:

Integrates \(g^{-1}\) over the normal random-effects distribution
Recovers the mean of the distribution of true effects
See Igelmann et al. (2026)

\[n_i \sim (\overline{n}/20) \times \chi_{df=4}^2 + (3\overline{n}/10),\]

where \(\overline{n}\) is the average sample size for a primary study and assuming equal group sizes Marín-Martínez and Sánchez-Meca (1998); Sanchez-Meca and Marin-Martinez (1998)

Generated observed CLES estimates (\(\hat{\theta}_i\)) implied by the model that

Conclusions and Discussion

Standard back-transformations are acceptable at low heterogeneity, but integral back-transformation is recommended when \(\tau_\theta\) is large
Under normality and homoscedasticity, SMD with integral back-transformation is the recommended

arcsine and logit transformations with the integral back-transformation were comparable across most conditions (except for coverage for moderate \(\tau_{\theta}\) and large \(k\))
Direct pooling should be avoided 

Next Study:

Extend to non-normal outcomes and unequal population variances and evaluate other estimates (and corresponding sampling variances) of stochastic superiority

Further Details on Between-study Heterogeneity

Specified \(\mu_{\theta}\) and \(\tau_{\theta}^2\) values as the moments of the beta distribution
Found the \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) parameters of the beta distribution by: \(\alpha = \mu_{\theta} \times \nu\) and \(\beta = (1 - \mu_{\theta})\nu\) where \(\nu = (\alpha + \beta) =\frac{\mu_{\theta}(1 - \mu_{\theta})}{\tau^2_{\theta}} - 1\).

Note. values must meet the following condition: \(\nu = (\alpha + \beta) > 0\), so therefore \(\tau^2_{\theta} < \mu_{\theta}(1 - \mu_{\theta})\)

For the specified \(\mu_{\theta}\) and \(\tau_{\theta}^2\), we derived them from SMD parameters through numerical integration

Obtaining CLES Estimates

After obtaining true CLES values, then transform to true SMD values:


\[
  g_{\text{d}}(\theta_i) = \Phi^{-1}(\theta_i)\sqrt{2}
  \]


Generate observed SMD estimates from a scaled non-central \(t\)-distribution assuming homoscedastic variances:


\[g_{\text{d}}(\hat{\theta_i}) \sim N\left(g_{\text{d}}(\theta_i),  \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}\right) \bigg/ \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2(df= n_1+n_2 -2)}{n_1 + n_2 -2}}\]
